name: Project health check
description: RAG status, late tasks, critical path, slips and over-allocated people — from your MS Project plan.

fields.label: Anything to focus on?
fields.placeholder: Optional — e.g. go-live date, the build phase

template:
Run a health check on the project plan {{plan}}. Focus: {{focus}}

Give me: overall RAG with a one-line reason; a 3-bullet summary; late or behind-schedule tasks (table); the critical path and how much float is left before go-live; the biggest slips vs. baseline; over-allocated people with suggested fixes; and the top 3 actions for this week.

name: Status report from my files
description: A send-ready status report built from your plan, budget tracker and RAID log.
template:
Write a status report for the {{audience}} using the project plan {{plan}}, the budget tracker {{budget}} and the RAID log {{raid}}.

Include: overall RAG plus schedule, budget, scope and resourcing RAGs; a 3-bullet executive summary; progress since last period; milestones (baseline vs. forecast); budget position (budget, actuals, forecast, variance, contingency left); top risks and issues with owners; decisions or help needed from the {{audience}}. Keep it to one page.

name: Update plan from progress sheet
description: Apply your team's % complete updates from Excel to the MS Project plan, then see what changed.
template: Update the project plan {{plan}} with the progress in {{progress}} and set the status date to {{status}}. Apply the changes (save as an updated copy), then give me a before/after table and tell me how the health of the plan changed: % complete, late tasks, forecast finish and anything that newly needs attention.

name: Plan → Excel tracker
description: Turn an MS Project plan into a colour-coded Excel tracker with a weekly Gantt chart that shows slips against the baseline.

fields.label: Earlier version of the plan, to show week-over-week change

template: Export the project plan {{plan}} to an Excel tracker with a variance Gantt chart. Earlier version to compare against: {{previous}} (if one is given, pass it as history; otherwise leave history out and Lumen compares with the versions it saved earlier). Name it after the project, ending in ' - Tracker.xlsx'. Then summarise what is in each sheet, and lead with the schedule variance: how many working days the forecast finish is behind the baseline, which milestones have slipped the most, and (if the tracker was compared with an earlier version) which milestones moved since then.

name: Who's overloaded?
description: Find over-allocated people in the next 6 weeks, and (with a capacity workbook) leave clashes, sprint overloads and estimate outliers, with options to fix them.
template:
Check resource loading in {{plan}} for the next six weeks. Team capacity workbook: {{capacity}}. Azure DevOps backlog export: {{backlog}}. (Leave out any that are blank.)

If there is a capacity workbook, call analyze_capacity with it, the plan and the backlog (weeks: 6) and base the answer on it: lead with anyone on leave during critical-path work, then overloaded weeks per person (Person · Week · Capacity · Demand · Over by · Tasks), overloaded sprints, and estimate outliers worth a second look. Mention data-quality gaps such as people missing from the capacity file. Without a capacity workbook, use analyze_project_plan and show each over-allocated person's peak load, dates and clashing tasks.

For each problem give two or three options to resolve it (move work, reassign, add help, change the leave cover), and for the most important one check the schedule impact with model_scenario. Do not change any files.

name: Budget variance review
description: Where you're over or under, contingency left, and invoices that need attention.
template: Review the budget workbook {{budget}}. Show total budget vs. forecast at completion, each category's variance (worst first), how much contingency is left, the monthly burn trend, and any invoices that are pending or unusual. End with three recommended actions.

name: Timesheets vs. plan
description: Compare hours booked in Excel with the work planned in MS Project.
template: Compare the hours in {{timesheets}} with the planned work and progress in {{plan}}. For each task, show the hours booked, the % complete in the plan, and whether effort looks higher than planned for the progress made. Highlight the top three effort overruns and what they mean for cost and schedule.

name: RAID log review
description: Top risks, overdue reviews and issues without a clear action — from your RAID workbook.
template: Review the RAID log {{raid}} as of {{asof}}. List the highest-scoring open risks, any risk or issue whose review or due date has passed, open issues without a clear action, and dependencies at risk. Suggest which ones to escalate to the steering committee.

name: Write user stories
description: Turn a feature idea into user stories with acceptance criteria.

fields.label: What's the feature or idea?
fields.placeholder: e.g. Customers can track their order status without calling support

name: Weekly status report
description: A crisp RAG status update ready to send.

name: Meeting notes → actions
description: Paste messy notes, get decisions, owners and next steps.

fields.label: Paste your meeting notes or transcript
fields.placeholder: Raw notes are fine — typos and all

name: Draft an email
description: Describe what you need to say — get a polished email.

fields.label: Who is it to?
fields.placeholder: e.g. My director, a vendor, the whole team

fields.label: What do you need to say?
fields.placeholder: e.g. The launch is slipping two weeks because of testing delays

name: Summarize a document
description: Attach a file and get the key points in seconds.
template:
Summarize the attached document {{file}}. Focus on: {{focus}}

Start with a one-line TL;DR, then key points, then anything that needs a decision or action.

name: Build a risk register
description: Identify likely risks with impact, likelihood and mitigations.

name: Explain it simply
description: Understand any technical term or concept in plain words.
template: Explain "{{topic}}" to a smart business professional with no technical background. Use an everyday analogy, then explain why it matters at work, then list 3 good questions I could ask an engineer about it.

name: Create a document
description: Have Lumen write a file into your project folder.

fields.label: What document do you need?
fields.placeholder: e.g. A one-page project charter for the new intranet

template:
Create this document and save it as a file in the current folder: {{what}}

Format: {{format}}. Choose a clear file name. When done, tell me the file name and give a short outline of what's inside.

name: Inventory the program knowledge
description: List the authoritative program documents, what each one settles, and where they disagree.

fields.label: Anything to focus on?
fields.placeholder: Optional — e.g. data model, integrations, release 1 scope

template:
Build an inventory of the program knowledge in my project folder (PID/scope, BRDs, Solution Blueprint, Ways of Working, data models and other program artifacts). Focus: {{focus}}

For each document give: name, type, version or last-modified date, what it is authoritative for, and its owner if stated. Then list the places where documents disagree or overlap (with citations), the gaps where nothing is authoritative, and the questions to settle with the program team.

name: Refine business requirements
description: Turn a BRD into atomic, testable requirements with IDs, acceptance criteria and sources.

fields.label: Which requirements?
fields.placeholder: Optional — e.g. BR-001 to BR-005, or the eligibility section

template:
Refine the business requirements in {{brd}}. Scope: {{scope}}

Check them against the scope document and other program knowledge in the folder. Give me a refined-requirements table (Req ID | Parent BR | Statement | Type | Acceptance criteria | Source | Status | Open questions), with Status set to Draft (AI). Then list ambiguities, conflicts between sources and missing requirements, each with a citation and who should answer it.

name: Draft the functional design
description: Behaviour, screens, business rules and data for approved requirements, traced by ID.

fields.label: Which requirements?
fields.placeholder: Optional — e.g. only Approved ones, or BR-002.*

template:
Draft the functional design for the requirements in {{reqs}}. Scope: {{scope}}

Use only approved requirements unless I've said otherwise, and ground the design in the Solution Blueprint and data model in my folder. Give me a functional-design table (FD ID | Title | Type | Description | Business rules | Traces To | Status), then error and edge cases, then a coverage check (every requirement in scope and the FD IDs that realise it), then open questions for the requirement owners.

name: Draft the technical design
description: Components, integrations, data changes and NFRs that realise the functional design.
template:
Draft the technical design for the functional design in {{fd}}. Scope: {{scope}}

Follow the Solution Blueprint and data model in my folder, and cite them. Give me a technical-design table (TD ID | Component | Approach | Interfaces / data | NFRs | Traces To | Status), then the integrations and data changes needed, the main technical risks with options and trade-offs, any departures from the Blueprint, and questions for the functional designer.

name: Write the backlog from the design
description: Epics, features and stories that implement the design, not the raw requirements.

fields.label: Which part?
fields.placeholder: Optional — e.g. the online application journey

template:
Write the delivery backlog for the design in {{design}}. Scope: {{scope}}

Use the Ways of Working in my folder for Definition of Ready and backlog conventions. Give me a backlog table (Item ID | Type | Title | Parent | Description | Acceptance criteria | Implements | Status) with epics, then features, then stories. Every story implements at least one FD or TD ID and has 3-6 Given/When/Then criteria. Finish with design elements that have no story yet, and any design gaps you found.

name: Traceability check
description: Coverage, gaps, broken links and stories that skip design, from your traceability workbook.
template:
Run a traceability check on {{trm}}.

Give me: overall RAG with a one-line reason; coverage per layer (table); then findings grouped by what someone must do (fix broken link, design missing, story needed, review after change, decide between conflicting items), each with IDs, cell references and a suggested owner; and the top 5 actions.

name: Impact of a requirement change
description: Everything downstream (design, stories) affected when a requirement changes.

fields.label: Which requirement IDs changed?
fields.placeholder: e.g. BR-004 (leave blank to use rows marked Changed)

fields.label: What changed?
fields.placeholder: Optional — e.g. eligibility age moved from 18 to 16

template:
Analyse the downstream impact of changed requirements in {{trm}}. Changed IDs: {{ids}}. What changed: {{change}}

For each changed requirement, list every affected refined requirement, functional design element, technical design element and story (with IDs and cells), say whether each one probably needs to change or only needs a review and why, mark the ones last updated before the change, and say who should review each layer. End with a proposed change-log entry.

name: My open work items
description: Everything assigned to you that isn't done, grouped by sprint, with what needs attention.
template: List the Azure DevOps work items assigned to me that are not closed, done or removed. Group them by sprint, then by state. Point out anything that looks stuck (no change in two weeks), anything blocked, and anything missing acceptance criteria or an estimate. End with what I should do first today.

name: Sprint status summary
description: Progress, risks and blockers in the current sprint.
template: Summarise the current sprint from Azure DevOps for {{audience}}. Lead with a RAG status and one line. Show counts by state (done, in progress, not started, blocked) and by type. List the items at risk of not finishing and why, unassigned items, and bugs raised this sprint. Link every item. Keep it to one screen.

name: Find it in the wiki
description: Answer a question from the Azure DevOps wiki, with the pages cited.

fields.label: What do you want to know?
fields.placeholder: e.g. How are renewal fees calculated for late renewals?

template:
Answer this from our Azure DevOps wiki: {{question}}

Search the wiki, read the most relevant pages, and answer in plain language. Cite each page as a link next to the point it supports. Say clearly if the wiki doesn't answer it or if pages disagree.

name: Stories from the design → Azure DevOps
description: Propose epics, features and stories in Azure DevOps from an approved design, traced by tags. You approve each batch.
template:
Create Azure DevOps work items for the approved design in {{design}}. Parent feature or epic, if given: {{parent}}.

First call ado_describe_work_item_type and check for existing epics and features with the same titles. Then propose the items with ado_propose_work_items: one story per design behaviour, each tagged with the FD/TD IDs it implements, with Given/When/Then acceptance criteria. Propose parents before children. Ask me for any required value you can't take from the design.

name: Publish a document to the wiki
description: Propose a wiki page from a Markdown or Word document. You review the diff and approve.
template: Publish {{doc}} to our Azure DevOps wiki at {{path}} (if no path is given, suggest one that fits the existing page tree). If the page exists, read it first and pass its etag. Keep headings, IDs and tables. Propose the page with ado_propose_wiki_page and tell me what changed compared with the current page.

name: Stale items check
description: Open work items with no change in a while, and what to do about each.

fields.label: No change for how many days?

template: Find open Azure DevOps work items (not closed, done or removed) with no change in the last {{days}} days. Work out the cut-off date from today's date and use changedBefore. Group them by owner. For each, suggest one action: close it, re-plan it, split it, or ask the owner. Link every item.

name: Release notes from closed items
description: Plain-language release notes from what was finished in a sprint.

fields.label: Which sprint? (optional)
fields.placeholder: Leave empty for the current sprint, or give an iteration path

template: Write release notes for business users from the Azure DevOps stories and bugs that are done or closed in this sprint: {{sprint}} (use the current sprint if empty). Group them as New, Improved and Fixed, one plain-language line each with a link. Leave out internal tasks.

name: Traceability against Azure DevOps
description: Check requirements and design in the TRM against the live backlog.
template: Check traceability against the live Azure DevOps backlog. Run ado_export_backlog with {{trm}} as the workbook, then analyze_traceability on the saved copy. Report coverage per layer, design elements with no story in Azure DevOps, stories with no lifecycle tags, and broken links, citing IDs and work item links. The original workbook must stay unchanged.

name: Weekly executive status
description: A draft status report and a one-page executive dashboard from your plan, RAID log and (optionally) Azure DevOps backlog export, with every fact traced to its source.
template:
Build this week's executive status pack for the project plan {{plan}} with the RAID log {{raid}} and the Azure DevOps backlog export {{backlog}} (leave out either if it is blank; pass the backlog export as backlog to both tools).

1. Call get_status_facts first and base everything on it.
2. Write a 3 to 5 sentence narrative for executives: the overall rating and why, what moved since last time, the biggest threat to the next milestone, delivery progress from the backlog if given, and what is being done. Use the calculated rating; if you think it should be different, say so as a recommendation, not as the rating.
3. List up to 3 decisions or support needed from leadership, each citing the task or RAID ID.
4. Call build_status_report with the narrative and decisions.

Then reply with the overall rating, the top 3 points, any warnings the tool returned, and links to the saved files. The tools read the newest approved RAID log automatically, so if raidInput has notes or pending huddle changes, tell me plainly which file was used and how many proposed RAID changes are still waiting for review (they are not in the pack). Remind me that the pack is a draft for PMO review.

name: Huddle → RAID log
description: Propose RAID log updates from a meeting transcript, each with the quote it came from, for you to approve before anything changes.
template:
Read the RAID log {{raid}} and the meeting transcript {{transcript}}. Take the meeting date from the transcript file name, or use today. Propose RAID updates with propose_raid_updates: updates and closures to existing items first, then new risks, issues, actions, decisions and dependencies. Quote the transcript word for word for each one, and do not invent owners or dates.

Then show me a table of the proposed changes with who said each one and when, anything that was not proposed and why, and the meeting checks. Tell me how to approve them.

name: Monthly plan change log
description: Compare the plan with an earlier version and list the changes, separating material schedule changes from administrative ones.

fields.label: Compare with the version from (optional)
fields.placeholder: e.g. 2026-10-01, or leave blank for the last saved version

template:
Produce the change log for the project plan {{plan}}, compared with the version from {{since}} (if blank, use the last saved version).

Call plan_change_log first and base everything on it. Then write:
1. A two-sentence headline: how many material changes, which milestones moved and by how many working days, and the project finish movement.
2. A table of material changes (ID · Task · What changed · Why it is material).
3. A short summary of the administrative changes, grouped by kind, without listing every row.
4. Anything the planner should confirm before this is published as the monthly baseline.
Only report what the tool returned.

name: Weekly look-ahead
description: What each workstream needs on its radar next week: starts, finishes, milestones, late work and dependencies.

fields.label: Workstream (optional)
fields.placeholder: e.g. Testing, or leave blank for all

template:
Write next week's look-ahead for the project plan {{plan}}, limited to the workstream {{workstream}} (if blank, cover every workstream).

Call plan_lookahead first and base everything on it. Open with the milestones and the 2 or 3 dependencies most likely to cause trouble. Then give one short section per workstream with what is starting, finishing and carried over late, and what it is waiting on and from whom. Keep it to one page that can be pasted into an email, and only report what the tool returned.

name: Update plan from ADO backlog
description: Propose plan % complete from an Azure DevOps backlog export, and list the data-quality gaps that stop it being reliable.
template:
Compare the Azure DevOps backlog {{backlog}} with the project plan {{plan}} (status date {{status}}; if blank, use the plan's).

1. Call plan_progress_from_backlog and base everything on it.
2. Show the proposed % complete changes as a table (ID · Task · Now · Proposed · Items done/total), and any that were held back because the backlog shows less progress than the plan.
3. Show the data-quality findings: unlinked items, links to missing or summary tasks, stale in-progress items, unknown states, and plan tasks that should be moving but have no backlog items. Say who needs to fix what.
4. Ask me to approve before changing anything. If I approve, call update_project_plan with only the approved rows and summarise what moved.

name: Delivery scenarios
description: Compare two or three "what if" scenarios (a slip, extra people, a dropped dependency) side by side: milestone movement, critical path and who gets overloaded.

fields.label: Scenarios to compare
fields.placeholder: e.g. A: UAT slips two weeks. B: ERP integration takes 10 more days but we add a half-time tester. C: start training before UAT sign-off.

template:
Compare these delivery scenarios for the project plan {{plan}}:

{{scenarios}}

1. Turn each scenario into model_scenario changes (durationDelta, startNoEarlierThan, resource + unitsDelta, removeDependency), naming tasks by ID. If a scenario is ambiguous, state the assumption you made.
2. Call model_scenario once per scenario, with its name. Base everything on what it returns.
3. Show a side-by-side table: Scenario · Go-live · Project finish · Milestones that move (working days) · Critical path changes · Newly over-allocated people. Then two or three lines per scenario on what drives the result.
4. Save the comparison with create_spreadsheet to "Scenarios/<today's date>.xlsx": a Comparison sheet (one row per scenario), a Milestones sheet (Scenario, Milestone, Before, After, Moved) and a Changes sheet (Scenario, Change).
5. Recommend one scenario and say why, as a recommendation. Nothing in the plan changes; if I approve a scenario, call update_project_plan with its planUpdates, which saves an "(updated)" copy.

name: Knowledge freshness
description: Which published Word/HTML snapshots are out of date with their source, which approved outputs were never published, and which snapshots are orphans. Good as a weekly scheduled check.

fields.label: Folders that should be published (optional)
fields.placeholder: e.g. Lifecycle, Wiki export — leave blank to check only what was published

template:
Check the freshness of the published knowledge in my project folder. Folders that should be published: {{sources}} (if blank, leave sources out).

Call check_freshness and base everything on it. Lead with one line: how many snapshots are stale, never published and orphaned. Then a table of stale snapshots (Snapshot · Source · Published version · Approved by · Published at · Source last changed), the approved sources never published, orphan snapshots, and anything missing. End with the actions to take and who should take them (re-approve then republish, publish, or remove). Do not change any files.

name: Generate test cases from stories
description: SIT and UAT test cases (positive, negative and boundary) from the stories' acceptance criteria, each tracing to its story and requirement, saved in the Azure DevOps Test Plans layout.

fields.label: Stories (traceability workbook, backlog export or stories document)
Which stories (optional)
fields.placeholder: e.g. US-101 to US-105, or leave blank for all

template:
Design test cases for the stories in {{stories}}, limited to {{scope}} (if blank, all live stories).

1. Read the stories, their Given/When/Then acceptance criteria and the design rules they implement.
2. For each criterion write a positive case, then negative and boundary cases for every limit and failure path. Each case: title, SIT or UAT, priority 1-4, preconditions and test data, numbered steps with one expected result each, and tracesTo with the story ID (and refined requirement where useful).
3. Show the cases as a table (ID, Title, Type, Priority, Traces to, Steps), then list acceptance criteria that can't be tested as written with a measurable rewording.
4. Save them with write_test_cases to "Test cases.xlsx" and tell me the file name and how many cases and steps it holds.

name: Coverage gaps
description: Requirements and stories with no test, and tests that trace to withdrawn items, from the Tests sheet of your traceability workbook.
template:
Check test coverage in {{trm}}.

Call analyze_traceability and base everything on it. Lead with test coverage per layer (requirements with tests, stories with tests) as a small table. Then list: requirements with no test, stories with no test, and tests tracing to withdrawn items (these should be retired or re-pointed), each with its ID and Sheet!Cell reference. Also list tests affected by changed requirements, which need review. End with the five most important tests to add, with the story or requirement each would cover. Do not change any files.

name: Draft the test strategy
description: Test Strategy / Master Test Plan from scope, requirements, plan and RAID: levels, environments, entry/exit criteria, test data and risk-based priority.
template:
Draft the Test Strategy and Master Test Plan from the scope {{scope}}, the requirements {{trm}}, the plan {{plan}} and the RAID log {{raid}} (skip any that are blank).

Sections: 1 Scope and out of scope; 2 Test levels and who runs them (unit, SIT, UAT, performance, accessibility, security); 3 Environments (STE, UAT, STG, PRD) and what runs where; 4 Entry and exit criteria per level; 5 Test data needs (synthetic or masked, never real personal data); 6 Defect management and severity definitions; 7 Schedule from the plan's test tasks and milestones; 8 Risk-based priority: a table of requirements with business impact, likelihood of failure, change impact (new, changed, or affected by a change) and the resulting priority (High/Medium/Low); 9 Testing risks from the RAID log; 10 Assumptions and open questions.

Cite the source for every fact. Label it 'Draft (AI) for review'. Do not save any files unless I ask.

name: Triage defects
description: Probable duplicates, severity–priority mismatches, ageing and unowned defects from a defect export, with changes proposed for your approval.
template:
Triage the defect export {{defects}} as of {{asof}} (if blank, today).

1. Call analyze_defects and base everything on it.
2. Lead with the summary line and counts by severity and state. Then tables: probable duplicates (Keep, Probable duplicate, Similarity, Area), severity-priority mismatches (Defect, Severity, Priority, Why it matters), the oldest open defects, and defects with no owner. Cite IDs and cells.
3. Show the proposed changes as a table (Defect, Field, Now, Proposed, Why) and ask me which to record. Only after I agree, call propose_defect_changes with the agreed rows and tell me how to approve them. Never change the original export.

name: Interview → change impacts
description: Propose change impacts from stakeholder interviews, each backed by a word-for-word quote, into a CIA workbook for you to approve.
template:
Read the CIA {{cia}} (if blank, there is none yet) and the interview transcript {{transcript}}. Take the interview date from the file name.

1. List the change impacts the interview supports: stakeholder group, roles if named, business process, the change in one sentence, level H/M/L, and a skill gap where it is clear. Skip impacts already in the CIA.
2. Propose them with propose_change_impacts (the CIA as cia if given). Quote the transcript word for word for each one; do not invent roles, headcounts or dates.

Then show me a table (ID, group, process, change, level, who said it and when), anything that was rejected and why, and the worries or risks raised that are not impacts. Tell me how to approve them.

name: Consolidate the CIA
description: Merge several Change Impact Assessments: duplicates merged, a heat map by stakeholder group and impact level, and the training needs.
template:
Consolidate these Change Impact Assessments: {{cia1}}, {{cia2}} and {{cia3}} (skip any that are blank), plus any other CIA workbooks I name, with the role list {{roles}} (skip it if blank).

Call consolidate_cia and base everything on it. Lead with the summary line. Then show: the duplicates merged (which IDs, and the level kept), the heat map as a table (group × High/Medium/Low with totals), the groups with the most high impacts, impacts still waiting for approval, and anything rejected or flagged in the notes. Give me links to the consolidated workbook and the training actions file, and remind me that the source workbooks were not changed.

name: Training needs analysis
description: Training needs by role from the consolidated CIA: skill gaps, training type, priority and headcount, with the training actions ready for Azure DevOps.
template:
Read the TNA and Consolidated impacts sheets of {{cia}}.

Write the Training Needs Analysis: 1 Summary (people affected by role and priority, using headcounts where given); 2 A table by role (role, group, headcount, skill gaps, training type, priority, impacts it comes from); 3 Recommended sequence (High first, and what must be ready before go-live); 4 Gaps: roles with no headcount, impacts with no skill gap, impacts not yet approved. Cite the sheet and row for every line. Then say how to bring the training actions into Azure DevOps (import the 'Training actions - ADO import.xlsx' file, or ask the Backlog Helper to propose them). Label it 'Draft (AI) for review'. Do not change any files.

name: Draft training materials
description: A role-based deck outline, job aid, FAQ and knowledge check from the approved impacts and TNA, each section citing its source.
template:
Draft training materials for the role {{role}} from the approved impacts and TNA in {{cia}} and the process document {{process}} (skip it if blank).

Produce: 1 a deck outline (one ## per slide, 3 to 5 bullets and speaker notes, 8 to 12 slides); 2 a one-page job aid (numbered steps for the new way of working); 3 an FAQ (8 to 12 questions); 4 a knowledge check (5 to 10 multiple-choice questions with the answer and why). End every section with 'Source:' and the sheet and row or document heading it is based on, and leave out anything you can't source.

Show the drafts, then save each one with save_draft_document under 'Training/{{role}}/' with word: true, listing its sources. Tell me the file names. Everything is a draft for the change lead.

name: Draft French version
description: A French draft of an approved English document using the EN/FR glossary, labelled machine-drafted for translator review, then checked.
template:
Read the glossary {{glossary}} and the approved English document {{english}}.

Draft the French version paragraph by paragraph: same headings and paragraphs in the same order, the glossary's French term every time, Do-not-translate terms kept, and numbers, dates, amounts and IDs copied exactly in French format. Save it with save_draft_document next to the English document, as '<name> (FR draft).docx', label 'Machine-drafted, needs translator review', sources = the English document. Then run check_terminology on the English document and your draft with the glossary, fix what it finds and save again if needed.

Reply with the file name, the check's headline, and any terms you were unsure about for the translator.

name: Bilingual QA
description: Check an English/French pair against the glossary: inconsistent terms, English left in the French, numbers and dates that differ, and missing paragraphs.
template:
Check {{french}} against {{english}} with the glossary {{glossary}}.

Call check_terminology and base everything on it. Lead with the headline. Then a table (Type · EN ¶ · FR ¶ · What differs · Suggested fix) with the excerpts, in this order: missing paragraphs, numbers/dates/IDs, terminology, untranslated English. End with a note that this is a machine check and a translator still reviews the French. Do not change either document.

name: Generate cutover checklist
description: Draft the cutover and rollback run-sheet from the deployment approach and the plan, in a layout the cutover status check can read.

fields.label: Cutover window
fields.placeholder: e.g. Sat 2 Jan 18:00 to Sun 3 Jan 06:00

template:
Draft the cutover and rollback checklist for the window {{window}}, from the deployment approach {{approach}} and the project plan {{plan}} (skip the plan if blank).

1. List the cutover steps in order: ID (C01, C02…), step, owner, planned start, planned end, depends on (step IDs), and how each step is verified. Include the go/no-go call, the freeze, data migration, integrations, smoke tests and the go-live confirmation.
2. List the rollback steps (R01…) with the trigger and the latest time the rollback decision can be made.
3. Save them with create_spreadsheet as "Cutover Run-sheet (draft).xlsx" with sheets Run-sheet and Rollback, using the columns ID, Step, Owner, Planned start, Planned end, Depends on, Actual start, Actual end, Forecast end, Status, Notes (times as YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM, Status Not started).

Take owners and times only from the documents; leave them blank where the documents don't say, and list those gaps at the end. Cite the section each step comes from.

name: Readiness check
description: Check the go-live readiness checklist: status by environment, missing evidence, overdue items and a Red/Amber/Green rating.
template:
Check release readiness using {{checklist}} as of {{asof}} (if blank, today).

Call check_readiness and base everything on it. Lead with the rating, its reasons and the rule. Then: missing evidence (item, the file it points to, cell), open must-have items, overdue items and items with no owner, and a table by environment (STE, UAT, STG, PRD: items, complete, open, missing evidence). End with what has to happen before go-live and who owns it. Do not mark anything as done.

name: Draft the runbook
description: Draft the operational runbook from the design, the deployment procedures and the support model, each section citing its source.
template:
Draft the operational runbook for {{system}} from the design {{design}}, the deployment procedures {{deploy}} and the support model {{support}} (skip any that are blank, and read other design documents in the notebook if they help).

Sections: overview and contacts, system context, routine operations (daily, weekly, monthly checks), monitoring and alerts, start-up and shut-down, backup and restore, common incidents and fixes, escalation and support hours, change and release steps. End each section with "Source:" and the document heading. Mark anything you can't source as To be confirmed.

Save it with save_draft_document as "Runbook - {{system}} (draft).md" with word: true, listing the source documents. Then tell me which sections still need input and from whom.

name: Cutover status update
description: A short status update from the cutover run-sheet: late steps, critical path, next steps and the projected finish. Repeat it every 30 minutes during the window.
template:
Give me a cutover status update from {{runsheet}} as of {{asof}} (if blank, now).

Call cutover_status with snapshot: true and base everything on it. Start with one line: the rating, steps done out of the total, and the projected finish against the planned finish. Then: late and blocked steps (step, owner, how late, cell), the critical path to the finish, and the next steps due in the next hour with who is waiting on whom. Keep it short enough to paste into the cutover bridge chat, and give me the link to the saved snapshot.

name: Hypercare closure report
description: Hypercare defect trends against the exit criteria, and a draft closure report with a recommendation.

fields.label: Exit criteria (optional)
fields.placeholder: One per line, e.g. No Sev1 open for 10 days. Optional

template:
Analyse hypercare from the defect export {{defects}} as of {{asof}} (if blank, today), against these exit criteria: {{criteria}} (if not specified, use the defaults).

1. Call hypercare_trends (each criterion as one item of exitCriteria) and analyze_defects, and base everything on them.
2. Lead with the verdict and each exit criterion with Pass/Fail and its evidence. Show the weekly trend as a table (week, opened, closed, open at week end, average age) and the open defects by severity with owners.
3. Draft the closure report: period and scope, trend, exit criteria, open defects and owners, recurring themes by area, the handover to business-as-usual support, and a recommendation (close, or extend until the failing criteria pass). Save it with save_draft_document as "Hypercare closure report (draft).md" with word: true, listing the export as the source.

Say Not ready to close while any criterion fails.

name: Architecture review
description: Review a design against the blueprint, the standards and the ADRs: a findings and deviation log, and a remediation backlog to import into Azure DevOps.

fields.label: Design to review (FDD, TDD or API spec)

template:
Review the design {{design}} against the blueprint {{blueprint}}, the ADRs in {{adrs}} and the data model {{model}} (skip any that are blank).

1. Call check_consistency with both documents (and the ADR folder and data model when given). Then read the sections the findings point to and check the design against the blueprint's principles and standards.
2. Lead with a short verdict and the three most important findings.
3. Findings and deviation log as a table: ID (AR-01…) · Finding · Type (Inconsistency, Deviation from standard, Superseded decision, Data model mismatch, Gap) · Severity · Evidence (file and heading, or ADR ID) · Recommendation.
4. Save the log with create_spreadsheet as "Architecture review - findings.xlsx", and the remediation backlog as "Architecture review - remediation (ADO import).xlsx" with columns ID, Work Item Type (Task), Title, Description (finding ID and evidence), Priority (1-4), Tags (Architecture).

Confirm each pattern-based finding in the text before you list it, and say when a document explains it. Do not change the design documents.

name: Draft an ADR
description: Draft an architecture decision record (MADR layout, status Proposed) from a decision discussion, numbered after the existing ADRs.
template:
Draft an ADR for "{{topic}}" from the discussion in {{notes}}.

1. Call index_adrs on {{adrs}} to find the next number and any ADR this decision replaces.
2. Write it in the MADR layout: title, status Proposed, date, context and problem statement, considered options (with pros and cons from the discussion), decision outcome, consequences (good and bad), and links. If it replaces an ADR, add "Supersedes ADR-nnn" and list the documents that still cite the old one.
3. Save it with save_draft_document as "{{adrs}}/ADR-nnn-<short-title>.md", listing the discussion as its source.

Use only what the discussion says; mark anything it doesn't settle as an open question. Leave the status as Proposed.

name: Reuse vs. build assessment
description: Check the reusable-asset register before building something new: fit, gaps, effort and a recommendation.

fields.label: What do we need?
fields.placeholder: e.g. Validate the mailing address on the renewal summary page

template:
We need: {{need}}

Read the reusable-asset register {{register}} and the design {{design}} (skip if blank). For each candidate asset give a table: Asset (cell) · What it does · Fit (Full, Partial, None) · Gaps · Effort to reuse · Effort to build. Then recommend reuse or build in one paragraph, preferring reuse unless a must-have gap rules it out, and name that gap. Cite the register cell or document heading for every fact. If the design proposes a build, say whether an ADR is needed to record the decision.

name: Assemble a gate pack
description: Build the stage-gate pack from the approved artefacts: a combined Word pack, the index with approval status and the open-item log.
template:
Assemble the gate pack from the gate definition {{gate}}, with the Word template {{template}} and the RAID log {{raid}} (skip any that are blank).

Call assemble_gate_pack and base everything on it. Lead with one line: ready or not ready for the gate, and why. Then a table of the artefacts (included or missing, file, version, approved by, date), the approvals still open, newer drafts that were left out because they are not approved, and the other open items. End with what has to happen before the gate and who owns it, where the documents say. Do not record any approval yourself.

name: Update technical inventory
description: Propose additions, changes and retirements to the technical inventory from delivery changes, for the owner to approve.
template:
Propose updates to the technical inventory {{inventory}} from the git log {{gitlog}}, the Azure DevOps export {{ado}} and the ADRs in {{adrs}} (skip any that are blank; you may add the design documents in the notebook).

Call propose_inventory_updates. Summarise the result as three short tables (to add, changed, to retire) with the evidence for each row (commit, work item, ADR or document heading). Point out anything that looks like a false match. End by reminding me to set Approve? on every row of the (proposed) copy; the inventory itself has not been changed.

name: Draft the SCTM
description: Map the control catalogue to the design: implementation statements that cite real FDD/TDD headings, saved as a (proposed) SCTM for the assessor, with remediation items for gaps.
template:
Draft SCTM rows for the controls in {{catalogue}}, based on the design {{design}} and the current SCTM {{sctm}} (skip it if blank).

1. Call analyze_controls with the catalogue, the SCTM and the design document. List the controls not yet mapped and the statements that need input.
2. Read the design and, for each control that is not mapped or needs input, draft an implementation statement only from what the design says, with the design reference set to the document and heading (e.g. "Technical Design - Security.md > 3.2 Encryption at rest"). If no heading covers it, write the question that needs answering and leave the design reference blank.
3. Call write_sctm with the rows, the catalogue and the design document, plus remediation items for any gaps.
4. Summarise: rows proposed, rows marked Needs input (with the question), rejected controls, and the remediation items.

Do not mark any control Implemented unless the documents say it is in place. The original SCTM must not change.

name: Security design document
description: Draft the Security Design Document from the architecture, the TDD and the SCTM, saved as Markdown and Word in the program template.
template:
Draft the Security Design Document from {{design}} and the SCTM {{sctm}}, in the Word template {{template}} (skip it if blank).

1. Call analyze_controls with the SCTM and the design document so you know which controls need input or are gaps.
2. Write the document: purpose and scope, system overview, security architecture (identity and access, logging and monitoring, data protection, network boundary, configuration and patching), control implementation summary by family (from the SCTM), residual risks and open items. Use the template's sections instead when it has them.
3. Cite the design heading or SCTM cell for each section. List controls marked Needs input or Gap as open items, not as in place.
4. Save it with save_draft_document as "Security Design Document.md" with word: true and the template, listing the sources.

name: Evidence gap check
description: Check the evidence folder against the SCTM: evidence found per control, missing, stale and orphan files, and a remediation list to import into Azure DevOps.
template:
Check the control evidence in {{evidence}} against the SCTM {{sctm}} and the catalogue {{catalogue}} (skip it if blank). Evidence older than {{days}} days is stale (365 if blank).

1. Call analyze_controls with the SCTM, the evidence folder, the catalogue and staleDays.
2. Lead with the counts: controls with evidence, missing, stale, orphan.
3. Tables of the missing evidence (control, what is missing, SCTM cell), the stale evidence (control, file, date, age) and the orphan files (file, suggested control). Report exactly what the tool found.
4. Save the evidence index and gap tracker with create_spreadsheet as "Evidence gap tracker.xlsx" (Control, Status, Evidence, Problem, Responsible party, Due), and the remediation list through write_sctm remediation items (one per missing or stale item and per gap).

Do not accept evidence or close gaps yourself.

name: Profile a dataset
description: Profile a CSV or Excel extract against the data dictionary: types, nulls, patterns, outliers and rule breaks with example rows, saved as a DQ findings report with scripts to re-run in Fabric.
template:
Profile the extract {{extract}} against the data dictionary {{dictionary}} (skip it if blank).

1. Call profile_data with the extract, the dictionary and scripts: true.
2. Lead with the counts: rows, columns, findings by severity.
3. A column profile table (column, type, null %, distinct, min, max, main pattern) and a findings table (column, rule, severity, count, example rows). Report exactly what the tool found.
4. For each High finding, suggest a fix at the source or a DQ rule for the pipeline.
5. Save the report with save_draft_document as "DQ findings - <extract name>.md" with word: true, including the PySpark and SQL profiling scripts in code blocks, and the extract and dictionary as sources.

Do not read the raw rows: refer to problems by column and row number.

name: Compare schemas
description: Reconcile a source schema with a target or canonical model: matched fields with type checks, fuzzy matches to confirm, and unmatched fields on both sides.

fields.label: Source schema (DDL, JSON Schema or dictionary)

template:
Compare the source schema {{source}} (table {{entity}}; all tables if blank) with the target schema {{target}}.

1. Call compare_schemas with the source, the target and sourceEntity.
2. Lead with the summary: matched (exact, normalized, fuzzy), type issues, unmatched on each side.
3. A table of matches (source field, target field, match, score, type check, note). Say for each fuzzy match whether the meaning fits.
4. Separate lists of the unmatched source fields and unmatched target fields, with a suggested way to handle each (derive, default, not migrated).
5. List the type conversions that need a decision.

name: Draft the STTM
description: Draft the source-to-target mapping workbook from the schema comparison, with transformation and DQ rules, unmatched fields marked Needs input and every row left as Draft for review.
template:
Draft the STTM from {{source}} (table {{entity}}; all tables if blank) to the {{layer}} model {{target}}.

1. Call compare_schemas with the source, the target and sourceEntity.
2. For each confirmed match, write a transformation rule in plain words (direct, trim, upper, parse date format 'yyyy-MM-dd', cast to decimal(10,2), default 'X', constant 'X', or expr: / sql:) and a DQ rule where the target is required or has allowed values. Note type conversions that need a decision.
3. Call write_sttm with path "STTM - <source> to {{layer}}.xlsx", the rows (target layer {{layer}}), and the source and target files with sourceEntity, so unmatched fields on both sides are added as Needs input.
4. Summarise: rows drafted, fuzzy matches to confirm, unmatched source and target fields (ask how to handle each).

Every row stays Draft. Ask the reviewer to set Status to Approved and add their name for each row they accept.

name: Generate pipeline code from the STTM
description: Generate PySpark, Spark SQL, pipeline JSON, unit tests and a reconciliation query for the approved STTM rows only, ready to review and run in a lower-environment Fabric workspace.
template:
Generate pipeline code from the approved rows of {{sttm}} for the {{layer}} layer (all layers if blank).

1. Call generate_pipeline_code with the STTM and the layer.
2. List the files written per target table, the rows code was generated for, and the rows refused (with the reason and cell).
3. List every TODO rule the generator could not translate, with a suggested expr: or sql: rule for the STTM.
4. Explain how to run it in a lower-environment Fabric workspace: notebook first, then the reconciliation query (row counts and checksums per layer), then the unit tests.

Do not generate code for rows that are not Approved, and do not change any row's status.
